title: Raising up vs. bringing down
core: All eleven move someone up or down a ladder — of office, of reputation, of worth. The elevating half differs mainly in **who does the raising** (an institution, a crowd, a patron, a private believer) and **how permanent it is**; the lowering half differs in **what actually gets taken** — the job, the rank, the quality, or just the audience's estimate. Almost none of them are about merit; they're about status being conferred or withdrawn by someone else. The trap is that a word can raise or lower a person without touching what they can actually do.

words.nuance: The only one pointed at the **future**: it names the next holder of a job, not the current worth of a reputation. It's also the most personal — one kingmaker (or, sneeringly, the man himself) does the choosing, where canonizing takes a committee and lionizing takes a crowd.

The ceiling of this group: the object is placed past the reach of criticism entirely, so no evidence can count against him. Unlike **lionize** (fuss) or **canonize** (paperwork), it's a claim about the worshippers' lost judgment — the sentence is usually an indictment of the fans, not a description of the idol.

Alone here in being about **noise rather than rank** — the parties, the profiles, the lecture tour. It confers no permanence and no authority: the same crowd that lionizes a novelist in spring drops her by autumn, whereas canonization is meant to be irreversible.

Requires an **institution with the standing to make it official** — the Church, the academy, the syllabus. Its distinctive effect is closure: the reputation is entered into the record and put beyond argument, which no amount of private veneration or public fêting can do.

The only one that is a **held attitude rather than a performed act** — nothing is announced, conferred, or written down. Its objects skew old and dead (founders, elders, relics), and the reverence sits just under worship, where **deify** goes over the line.

Strips a **ruler of the office itself** — throne, presidency, party leadership — and says nothing about esteem; a deposed king may still be venerated. It is the coldest, most procedural word on the lowering side: a no-confidence vote deposes as surely as a tank column does.

The generic **removal from a seat**, at any altitude — CEO, board member, incumbent, tenant. Where **depose** insists on rank and formality, oust leaves the method entirely open and lives in the newsroom passive: *was ousted*, agent unnamed.

Doesn't remove anyone — it **moves them down to a stated worse place**, and the sentence almost always carries the destination: *to the bench, to a footnote, to the second division*. It's also the most comfortable with inanimate objects: a theory or a language can be relegated, but not deposed or ousted.

Attacks the **substance rather than the position**: the coin, the currency, the language, the office keeps its name and face value while its actual worth is diluted. It always implies a prior standard that was corrupted, which is why it can be done by the holder to himself.

Purely a **speech act** — it changes nobody's rank, only how small the thing sounds. No power is required beyond a condescending tone, and the technique is calm dismissal (*it wasn't that hard*), not the institutional shove of marginalizing or the removal of ousting.

Leaves the target **present but unheard** — still in the room, still on the payroll, structurally irrelevant. Uniquely, it often has **no actor at all**: defaults and habits do it, where belittling needs a speaker and ousting needs a decision.

exam_note: The up/down split is too easy to be the test; the exam works inside one half — asking whether the lowering verb took the office (**depose**, **oust**), the rank (**relegate**), the quality (**debase**), or only the audience's opinion (**belittle**, **marginalize**), and whether the exalting was done by an institution (**canonize**), a crowd (**lionize**), a patron (**anoint**), or a believer (**venerate**, **deify**).
